title: Mixed-priority warm-cache efficiency notes
content:
Goal: quick scratchpad to record experiments probing how mixed-priority traffic shapes warm-KV-cache efficiency and resulting latency tail behavior. High-level hypothesis: a small fraction of high-priority short requests can keep the KV cache skewed toward small prefixes and reduce hit-rate for large requests, increasing p95/p99 on low-priority large batches.

Environment / harness:
- Runtime: local dedicated node (A10G like profile), single serving process, quantized ggml-ish model with KV cache enabled.
- Harness: synthetic driver with two workload generators: HP (high-priority) short sequence length S~[8..32], LP (low-priority) long sequences L~[256..1024].
- Arrival: Poisson mix, overall lambda adjusted for 2000 rps target.
- Prewarm: 500s of LP-only warm to fill KV, then flip to mixed.
- Batching policy: dynamic batching with 40ms max wait.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, KV hit ratio (per-seq-length buckets), batch size distribution, CPU/GPU utilization.

Experiment matrix (not exhaustive):
1) Baseline LP-only warm then steady LP-only at 2000 rps (control).
2) Mix A: HP fraction 5% (burst-like), rest LP.
3) Mix B: HP fraction 20% continuous.
4) Priority preemption ON/OFF (preempt HP over LP when queued).

Key observations (raw):
- Baseline: KV hit ratio for L sequences stabilizes at ~0.86 after warm; p95 ~ 230ms, p99 ~ 480ms.
- Mix A (5% HP): Within 2 minutes of switching, KV hit ratio for L drops to ~0.72; p95 increases to 310ms, p99 to 760ms. Notable increase in small-batch frequency due to HP merging rules.
- Mix B (20% HP): KV-L hit ratio falls to ~0.58; p95 ~ 410ms, p99 > 1.2s. Throughput maintained but jitter high.
- With preemption enabled: observed improved HP latencies (p95 < 60ms) but LP p99 worsened marginally compared to non-preempted Mix B (preemption moves LP work later causing colder cache effects).

Micro-insights: 
- HP requests tend to evict the tail of the KV cache because their short prefixes map to hot cache slots; eviction policy currently LRU-ish and strong temporal locality assumption breaks with mixed sizes.
- Batching: HP presence increases occurrence of small batches since batching heuristics emit early to satisfy HP; small batches hurt LP amortization and token-level efficiency.
- Prewarming shape matters: warm with mixed traffic reduces the initial hit loss but steady-state still degrades vs LP-only warm.

Quick ASCII trend (KV-L hit ratio over time, example Mix A):
[time] 0m  2m  4m  6m  8m
[hit] 0.86 0.78 0.73 0.71 0.72

Notes on instrumentation gaps:
- Need per-key hotness traces (not just seq-length buckets) to verify eviction hotspots.
- Batch composition exporter currently coarse: record per-batch types (HP/LP mix) and average seq length.

Immediate action items / next runs:
- Try alternate eviction: freq-weighted LRU (give small prefixes lower eviction priority) and re-run Mix B.
- Experiment with batching window differentiation by priority: allow HP to bypass but not force batch flush on LP-critical lanes.
- Run long 6h stability run with traffic ramp to observe steady-state eviction oscillations.
- Add a lightweight sampler to log actual KV keys evicted for a subset of requests (privacy-safe synthetic keys).

Conclusions so far (working):
- Mixed-priority traffic materially reduces warm-KV benefit for long sequences, increasing tail latencies for LP requests.
- Preemption helps HP latencies but can make LP tails worse; there's a trade-off.
- Mitigations look promising: tuned eviction + priority-aware batching.

Questions to discuss with Samir / Lena:
- Acceptable LP p99 threshold when HP% is X? (we need product guidance)
- Would product prefer HP SLAs at cost of LP tails or more even fairness?

Scratch log ends. Save configs and raw traces under /shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/benchmarks/mixed-priority/ (TODO move), link above.
